name: Ironmarrow Work Armor
description: Heavy, deliberate, built to take punishment. The centerpiece is a long-sleeved work shirt in dense slate-grey canvas with a mandarin collar, the fabric doubled at the shoulders and elbows with fused patches of scrap ballistic weave — grey-black, slightly shinier than the base cloth, creating a subtle armored texture. Over it goes a full-bib dungaree in dark charcoal, the chest panel reinforced with a sewn-in plate of recovered polycarbonate sheeting — not enough to stop a round but enough to matter in a knife situation or industrial accident. The left bib strap has been replaced with a length of riveted leather, darker and stiffer than the original. Wide-leg construction allows movement and accommodates a right-leg chrome prosthetic: the outer seam of the right leg is left open and fitted with heavy-duty snaps so it can be peeled back for maintenance access without removing the garment. Boots are tall, steel-toed, lace-up in cracked black leather with a composite platform sole — resoled with industrial conveyor belt rubber, grippy and virtually indestructible. A cloth balaclava in faded rust-brown is shoved into a chest pocket. The hands are covered by thick work gloves with the fingertips cut away on three fingers of the right hand for manual dexterity. A wide leather tool belt hangs across the hips, hung with a multi-tool, two carabiners, and a looped length of safety cord.
functionality: Ballistic weave shoulder and elbow patches reduce abrasion and impact damage. Polycarbonate bib insert provides soft-body-armor-equivalent frontal protection against blades. Right-leg snap seam allows chrome prosthetic access and maintenance. Steel toe boots protect against industrial hazards. Tool belt carries essential equipment. Balaclava deployable for respiratory or identity protection.
what_it_says: This person works — hard, dangerous, physical work. They've been hurt before and built their clothing to prevent it happening the same way twice. The chrome prosthetic accommodation isn't hidden; it's practical. There's a certain authority to this look, a the Gray Zone-level toughness that says the wearer has survived things that would break most people, and they're still showing up.
worn_by: people with chrome prosthetics who need functional aug-compatible gear
manufacturer: Self-constructed; canvas sourced from industrial surplus markets
story_hooks: The polycarbonate bib plate has a partial corporate logo still visible under the paint — from a facility that was supposedly decommissioned years ago.

The chrome leg prosthetic the outfit was built around is getting a rejection signal from the wearer's body, and they need either new chrome or a black-market medtech before the seam they built their whole wardrobe around becomes irrelevant.
The tool belt's multi-tool was passed down from the wearer's parent — and it has a data chip embedded in the handle that neither of them ever knew about.

physical_description.visual_profile: Imposing, utilitarian silhouette — broad shoulders tapered by reinforced panels, long and angular from waist to ankles. The garment reads as protective fortification rather than fashion: industrial, deliberately scarred, built for survival in harsh environments. A person in this outfit appears grounded, capable, ready for physical labor or conflict.
physical_description.fit: Deliberately oversized through the torso and thighs, allowing layering and unobstructed movement. The chest and shoulders are structured by fused ballistic patches that create subtle bulk. Right leg is wide and loose to accommodate chrome prosthetic; left leg tapers slightly toward the boot cuff.
physical_description.primary_material: Dense slate-grey canvas (base), charcoal dungaree twill, grey-black ballistic weave patches (shoulder/elbow reinforcement), recovered polycarbonate sheeting (chest plate), dark leather (bib strap, tool belt, gloves), black leather boots, industrial conveyor belt rubber (sole), rust-brown cotton (balaclava)
physical_description.texture: Rough and tactile — heavy canvas with visible weave, fused patches create subtle armor-like ridges and sheen variation, leather is cracked and supple from use, polycarbonate plate is matte and rigid, rubber sole is deeply grooved and gripping
physical_description.color_scheme: Slate-grey and charcoal foundation with grey-black ballistic accents; dark brown leather providing warmth and contrast; rust-brown balaclava adds historical decay aesthetic; steel-grey metal hardware (rivets, snaps, carabiners) scattered throughout
physical_description.closures: Heavy-duty snaps (right leg seam access), rivet stitching (leather bib strap), lace-up boots with thick cordage, friction-fit tool belt, carabiners securing cords
distinctive_features: Fused ballistic weave patches at shoulders and elbows — dual-layer armor aesthetic
Polycarbonate chest plate sewn into dungaree bib — visible protective panel
Right leg open seams with industrial snaps for prosthetic access and maintenance
Riveted leather bib strap replacing original fabric — marks of custom repair
Cut-away fingerless right-hand glove fingers for dexterity
Tool belt with multi-tool, carabiners, safety cord — working utility integrated into garment
Tall steel-toed boots with industrial conveyor belt resole
Rust-brown balaclava stowed in chest pocket — ready-access face protection
Visible wear: creased canvas, weathered leather, scuff patterns on reinforced zones
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 4-5 functional salvage — self-constructed from industrial surplus, no luxury markers, built for survival and hard labor rather than status
physical_description.cultural_context: Street engineer, industrial salvage worker, or dockside maintainer. Signals competence, scarcity mindset, and willingness to work dangerous jobs. The chrome prosthetic visibility (via accessible snaps) indicates visible augmentation — common among working-class GLMZ residents who can't afford invisible subcutaneous tech. This is worn by people who fix things, move things, survive things.
physical_description.condition_typical: Perpetually weathered — creases in the canvas from repeated bending, scuffed polycarbonate plate, salt stains on leather, worn brass rivets, frayed lace ends, grease and grime settling into seams. Each piece looks broken-in and jury-rigged, maintained through necessity rather than aesthetics.
